scenes.vo: Here's the plan. What impermanent loss actually measures, and the formula behind it. The full L.P. profit and loss formula, every real component, not just the headline number. A complete worked example, with real numbers, from entry to a real price move. And the one honest question that separates a good LP decision from a lucky market.

scenes.title: Lagging simply holding
scenes.sub: Not a loss in isolation. A comparison.
scenes.vo: What IL actually measures.

lines: Not measured against zero — against never depositing.
scenes.sub: A comparison, not a loss in isolation.
scenes.vo: Here's the precise definition, worth getting exactly right, since the name itself is easy to misread. Impermanent loss is how much your L.P. position lags simply holding the same starting tokens, once their relative price has changed. It isn't measured against zero. It's measured against the specific alternative of never having deposited at all.

Here's exactly why the name includes “impermanent.” The gap between your L.P. position and simply holding only becomes a real, locked-in loss the moment you withdraw. If the price ratio moves back to where it started before you withdraw, that gap closes completely, back to zero. Withdraw while the ratio is still different from your entry, and what was impermanent becomes permanent, instantly.

scenes.title: The IL formula, in two numbers

nodes.label: r = new price ÷ entry price
nodes.sub: The one input the formula needs
Turns it into a percentage lag

nodes.label: = impermanent loss
nodes.sub: Before fees, before gas, before anything else

scenes.vo: Here's the formula itself, broken into the two numbers it actually needs. Take r, the new price divided by your entry price. Impermanent loss equals two times the square root of r, divided by one plus r, minus one. Feed in any price ratio, and this formula alone tells you the percentage lag, before fees, before gas, before anything else.

scenes.title: When ETH rises vs falls
scenes.vo: Worth knowing this formula doesn't care which direction price moves, only how far the ratio has diverged. E.T.H. rising from three thousand to four thousand, a ratio of one point three three, gives about negative one percent. E.T.H. falling from three thousand to two thousand two hundred fifty, the exact reciprocal ratio, gives that same negative one percent. Divergence causes it, in either direction, symmetrically.

scenes.title: Impermanent loss, as price ratio diverges
scenes.sub: Illustrative shape — symmetric in both directions
scenes.vo: Plot the formula across a wider range of price moves, and the shape makes the “either direction” point obvious. Barely any divergence, barely any impermanent loss. As the ratio moves further from one, in either direction, the loss grows, and it grows faster the further you go, the same bending-curve shape from Lesson two point two, just applied to your total position now, not a single trade.

scenes.q: ETH doubles in price. What's the impermanent loss on a 50/50 pool, from the formula?
scenes.vo: Quick check. E.T.H. doubles in price. What's the impermanent loss on a fifty-fifty pool, from the formula? [[pause 4]] The answer: about negative five point seven percent, versus simply holding. r equals two, and the formula gives two root two over three, minus one.

scenes.title: Every real component, not just the headline
scenes.vo: Full LP P&L.

scenes.title: Every component, added up honestly

nodes.label: + Incentive rewards
nodes.sub: Any extra the protocol paid you

scenes.vo: Here's the full formula, every component that actually determines whether L.P.ing was worth it. Start with your L.P. position's current value, which already has impermanent loss baked into it. Add every fee you've earned along the way. Add any extra incentive rewards the protocol paid you. Subtract gas, for depositing, and for withdrawing. And that total is what you actually compare against simply holding, not any single piece of it alone.

lines: Up 20% since deposit means nothing alone.
It could be entirely the tokens rising.
scenes.sub: LPing itself could still have cost you, once compared honestly.
scenes.vo: Worth naming the trap this full formula exists to close. Looking only at your L.P. position's dollar value today, up twenty percent since you deposited, tells you almost nothing on its own. That twenty percent could be entirely the underlying tokens rising in price, with L.P.ing itself having actively cost you, once compared honestly against simply holding those same tokens.

scenes.title: Tracking this weekly, in practice
steps: LP value and implied price ratio, same day each week
Fees and incentives earned, recorded separately
What simply holding would be worth today, as the benchmark
scenes.result: Same three numbers, every single week
scenes.vo: Here's how to actually track this weekly, in practice, not just in theory. Record your L.P. position's current value, and the price ratio it implies, every week, on the same day. Record fees and any incentive rewards earned since the last check-in, separately from the position value. And calculate what simply holding your original deposit would be worth today, as the one number everything else gets judged against.

scenes.title: The same gas on $6,000 vs $600

right.label: $20 gas, on $600
items: Can wipe out a modest fee APR alone

scenes.vo: One more honest factor the full formula surfaces: gas matters far more, proportionally, on a small position than a large one. Twenty dollars of combined gas on a six-thousand-dollar position is about a third of a percent, a real but small drag. That same twenty dollars on a six-hundred-dollar position is over three percent, enough on its own to wipe out a modest fee APR before anything else is even counted.

scenes.q: Your LP is up 20% since deposit. Did LPing work?
scenes.a: Unknown until you compare with holding — the 20% could be all price.
scenes.vo: Quick check. Your LP position is up twenty percent since you deposited. Did LPing itself work? [[pause 4]] The answer: unknown, until you compare it with simply holding the same tokens. That twenty percent could be entirely from the price rising, not from LPing.

scenes.title: 1 ETH + 3,000 USDC, ETH to $4,000
scenes.vo: Worked example.

Here's the starting position this entire worked example runs on. One E.T.H., plus three thousand U.S.D.C., deposited at an E.T.H. price of three thousand dollars. Total starting value: six thousand dollars, split evenly between the two.
scenes.cap: Here's the starting position this entire worked example runs on. 1 ETH, plus 3,000 USDC, deposited at an ETH price of $3,000. Total starting value: $6,000, split evenly between the two.

scenes.title: What the pool does as ETH rises to $4,000
scenes.vo: Now E.T.H. rises to four thousand dollars, and follow exactly what the pool does to your position. It rebalances you to zero point eight six six E.T.H., and three thousand four hundred sixty-four U.S.D.C., by the same constant-product formula from Lesson two point two. Your L.P. position's value: zero point eight six six times four thousand, plus three thousand four hundred sixty-four, comes to six thousand nine hundred twenty-eight dollars.

scenes.title: LP value alone vs the full total
scenes.vo: Now add fees and gas, the parts a bare impermanent-loss number always leaves out. This position earned one hundred fifty dollars in fees along the way, and cost twenty dollars in gas, for depositing and withdrawing combined. LP total, all in: six thousand nine hundred twenty-eight, plus one hundred fifty, minus twenty, comes to seven thousand fifty-eight dollars.

stats: vs starting $6,000 — mostly ETH rising, not LPing
vs simply holding — the value LPing itself added
scenes.vo: Now compare that seven thousand fifty-eight dollars against two different baselines, since only one of them actually judges the LPing decision. Against your starting six thousand dollars, you're up one thousand fifty-eight, which is mostly E.T.H. simply rising in price. Against simply holding, seven thousand dollars, you're up only fifty-eight dollars. That fifty-eight dollars, not the one thousand fifty-eight, is the actual value LPing itself added.
scenes.cap: Now compare that $7,058 against two different baselines, since only one of them actually judges the LPing decision. Against your starting $6,000, you're up $1,058, which is mostly ETH simply rising in price. Against simply holding, $7,000, you're up only $58. That $58, not the $1,058, is the actual value LPing itself added.

lines: Not the $1,058. That part wasn't earned.
scenes.sub: The market move isn't a skill. Beating holding is.
scenes.vo: So here's the one sentence a master actually judges this position on, and it isn't the bigger number. A master judges the L.P. on the fifty-eight dollars, not the one thousand fifty-eight. The market move isn't a skill. Beating simply holding, even by a little, is the only part that was actually earned.

scenes.kicker: What could have gone the other way
lines: Lower fees could have meant a real loss.
Fee income has to outrun the IL, every time.
scenes.sub: The same price move, a different fee outcome, a different verdict.
scenes.vo: Worth naming what could have gone the other way in this exact same worked example, since a positive fifty-eight dollars was not guaranteed. If thirty-day volume had been lower, fees earned might have been thirty dollars instead of one hundred fifty, which would have left this position at negative sixty-two dollars against simply holding, a real loss from LPing, on the very same price move. The fee income is what has to outrun the impermanent loss, not the other way around.

scenes.q: When does impermanent loss actually become a permanent, locked-in loss?
scenes.a: When you withdraw while the price ratio is still different from entry.
scenes.vo: Quick check. When does impermanent loss actually become a permanent, locked-in loss? [[pause 4]] The answer: the moment you withdraw while the price ratio is still different from your entry ratio. If it moves back to entry first, the gap closes completely.

scenes.title: Your checklist
steps: Record IL, fees, incentives and gas separately
Exit if fees consistently fail to cover IL
scenes.vo: Here's your checklist. Do it now, and keep doing it weekly. Track your P&L against simply holding, every week, not just once at the end. Record impermanent loss, fees, incentives and gas separately, not as one blended number. And write your exit rule now: if fees consistently fail to cover impermanent loss, that's your signal to leave, not a reason to wait it out.

scenes.title: Recap
items: IL: how far an LP position lags simply holding
Full LP P&L: LP value + fees + incentives − gas, vs holding
The worked example: +$1,058 vs starting, but only +$58 vs holding
Judge the LP on the $58 — the market move isn't a skill
scenes.vo: Let's recap. Impermanent loss measures how far your LP position lags simply holding, once price has moved, and it's only permanent once you withdraw. Full LP P&L is LP value, plus fees, plus incentives, minus gas, compared honestly against holding. In the worked example, a thousand-dollar-plus gain was mostly the market; only fifty-eight dollars was actually earned by LPing. And that fifty-eight dollars, not the bigger number, is what a master actually judges the position on.
Track your P&L against simply holding, every week, and judge yourself on what LPing actually added. Next up, Lesson two point five: MEV and protecting your trades.
